Senses.Explanation: To live and die together is to share the same exposure in a Chan encounter: the master calls for someone who will stand with him through the case rather than remain a spectator. Dahui Zonggao asks whether anyone will live and die together with him, then calls that person out to meet his staff. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise asks for a patch-robed monk who will do so after raising Fengxue’s opposed alternatives. These are public challenges, not descriptions of two people sharing dates of birth and death. Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to a teacher who enters the same cauldron and furnace as the person being freed, and elsewhere to going through the fire sermon with the buddhas of the three times. Yunwai Ze uses it in a memorial address but immediately refuses to let the phrase pass without a further test. An unnamed monk asks Fushan Dexuan directly what living and dying together is; Fushan turns the question back on whether the monk may be called Buddha. The sources repeatedly mark shared exposure, accompaniment, or matched commitment under a live test. They do not make the phrase a promise of literal simultaneous death, nor do they supply one abstract theory behind every case.

ModifierControls.Control: 同 governs both 生 and 死
ModifierControls.Finding: The translation keeps togetherness across both poles; neither half is treated as a separate temporal claim.

FamilyControls.Finding: The Xuefeng–Yantou formula distinguishes sharing one line in birth from sharing one line in death; it is related but lexically more specific.
Life and death alone names the broader pair; this entry adds the relational demand to share them.
Meeting supplies the live encounter in Dahui’s challenge but is not synonymous with the solidarity formula.
